note: Representative installations for the terminal-phase lab. This is not a target list and no state's plan is claimed for any of it: each entry is a real, publicly known place of its kind, put here so that a weapon of a stated yield and accuracy can be flown at something with a shape and a hardness rather than at an abstraction. Positions are from public sources and are given to about a hundred metres where the installation is openly mapped, and to a kilometre or so where it is known by name and region only; the tier on each entry says which. Hardness is the class hardness from the accuracy lab and is modelled, not measured.
source: Positions: OpenStreetMap and the installations' own published locations, cross-read against the Nuclear Notebook (Kristensen, Korda, Johns and Knight, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists) and FAS Nuclear Information Project where those name a place. Hardness classes: Office of Technology Assessment (1979); Glasstone and Dolan (1977); Cochran, Arkin and Hoenig, Nuclear Weapons Databook.

dockyard.name: Dockyard
dockyard.note: A submarine or fleet base. Soft: what fails here is what is alongside, and the piers and sheds go with it. A boat at sea is not on this list, which is the whole argument for putting them there.

command.name: Command centre
command.note: A national or theatre command post. The deep ones are a figure of merit rather than a design: at ten thousand pounds per square inch only a crater reaches the target, and the overpressure rule overstates what a near miss does.

radar.name: Early-warning radar
radar.note: A ballistic-missile early-warning set. Large, fixed, soft, and the first thing a side that means to strike first would want off the air — which is why attacking one has always been read as the opening move rather than a raid.
